cards.question: Which destructor is absent after an owner's constructor body throws?
cards.answer: The not-fully-constructed owner's destructor. Already constructed member objects are still destroyed in reverse construction order.

cards.question: What cleanup runs if constructing the second member fails?
cards.answer: Only subobjects that completed construction are destroyed. The failing member and incomplete owner do not have their destructors called.

cards.question: Why does a construction log need both start and finish meaning?
cards.answer: A message before a possible throw does not prove construction completed. Define what each logged event actually witnesses.

cards.question: Why prefer lifetime-managed resources in a throwing constructor?
cards.answer: Completed owning members clean themselves up during unwinding. Manually held resources are easier to leak before the owner becomes fully constructed.

cards.question: What must std::string cleanupTrace(bool fail) accept and reject?
cards.answer: Record member construction A+, B+, then owner body. On success record owner-, B-, A-. If the owner body throws, record B-, A-, caught with no owner- entry. Return the entries joined by single spaces.

cards.question: Predict the output: Trace cleanup of incomplete construction. Assume the required standard-library headers; the function and sample main are shown.
cards.answer:
A+ B+ body B- A- caught
Why: The log outlives the owner and its members. Actual constructors and destructors produce the trace, so the evidence follows the language cleanup rules.

cards.question: What is wrong with this starter for Trace cleanup of incomplete construction?
cards.answer: The starter includes owner- on failure, claiming destruction of an object that never completed construction. Repair: Completed members are destroyed in reverse order. An owner whose constructor throws never runs its own destructor.

cards.question: What must stay true while implementing Trace cleanup of incomplete construction?
cards.answer: Completed members are destroyed in reverse order. An owner whose constructor throws never runs its own destructor.

cards.question: Why was this design selected for Trace cleanup of incomplete construction?
cards.answer: The log outlives the owner and its members. Actual constructors and destructors produce the trace, so the evidence follows the language cleanup rules.

cards.question: Which competing design could solve Trace cleanup of incomplete construction, and when is it useful?
cards.answer: A hard-coded trace can predict one case but does not demonstrate real cleanup. Production cleanup should use a nonthrowing logging policy; this bounded test assumes log allocation succeeds.

topics.title: Interpret the result
topics.summary: The first path is ordinary stack unwinding for a completed local owner. The second path is cleanup of already-constructed subobjects when the full construction fails. The example does not invoke an enclosing destructor for an object whose construction never completed, and it does not rely on abrupt process termination running C++ cleanup.

blocks.text: The test is small enough to trace with a counter, but the ownership lesson is broader. A resource acquired as an owning member can remain protected during later construction failure. A raw acquisition whose release exists only in the enclosing destructor may not have that protection. Book II develops this relationship into general RAII design.
